passage: In class, Damini, five, held up her painting. Lalremsiami Ma'am was busy with the register and said flatly, "Good job," without looking up. Damini's smile dropped and she put the painting down. Later Lalremsiami came to her desk and crouched. "You used the yellow all the way to the edge, and you made the sun with rays. That took patience." Damini sat up. "I did rays!"

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami say about the yellow?
qa.a: That Damini used it all the way to the edge.

qa.q: How did Damini feel after "Good job" said flatly, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Deflated and unsure the teacher had really looked, shown by her dropping smile. She might also just have been tired.

qa.q: What made the second comment land better?
qa.a: It named exactly what Damini did, the yellow to the edge and the rays, and was said face to face.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel when she notices Damini's face?
qa.a: Probably a little regretful about rushing, and glad to put it right. She came to the desk to look properly.

grounding: Shows a young child reading a flat good job as empty and specific praise as meaningful.

passage: I'm Ankita, Jyoti's cousin. Jyoti, five, ran to her aunt with a block tower. "Look!" Auntie, on the phone, said "Nice" in a flat voice. Jyoti knocked the tower down slowly. Then Uncle sat on the floor beside her. "You put the big ones at the bottom so it doesn't fall!" Jyoti beamed and started stacking another.

qa.q: What did Uncle say about the big blocks?
qa.a: That she put the big ones at the bottom so it doesn't fall.

qa.q: Why might Jyoti have knocked the tower down slowly?
qa.a: Possibly disappointment that the flat "Nice" did not show her tower had been seen. She might also just have been finished with it.

qa.q: How can adults make praise mean more to a child like Jyoti?
qa.a: Say specifically what the child did, like the big blocks at the bottom, with a warm face.

qa.q: How might Auntie see her "Nice"?
qa.a: She likely meant a quick kindness while busy on the phone, without realising it sounded empty to Jyoti.

grounding: Shows a child reading flat praise as empty and specific praise as landing, seen by an older cousin.

passage:
Monday: Divyansh held up his drawing of a train. Disha, scrolling on her phone, said flatly, “Good job.” Divyansh looked at her face, then folded the drawing and put it in the drawer.
Wednesday: He showed her a block tower. Disha put her phone down and smiled. “You used all the long blocks at the bottom so it doesn't wobble!” Divyansh's eyes lit up. “Yes! I thought of that.”
Friday: He brought her three drawings in a row, explaining each one.

qa.q: What did Divyansh draw on Monday?
qa.a: A train.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he folded the drawing and put it away?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and unseen, because the flat “Good job” and her eyes on the phone didn't feel like real interest.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday that made the praise land?
qa.a: Disha looked at him, smiled, and said something specific about what he did, the long blocks at the bottom.

qa.q: How might Disha feel on Friday when he brings three drawings?
qa.a: She likely feels happy and a little moved that he now wants to share his work with her.

grounding: Over a week, a child reads flat praise as empty and responds warmly to a smile and specific words.

passage: The power had been out all evening, and Vishal came home after a twelve-hour shift, soaked from the rain. Preeti rushed to him in the candlelight. “Papa, look! I tied my shoelaces myself!” Vishal, dropping onto the sofa, said, “Hmm, good,” without looking. Preeti's smile faded. She sat down slowly. Vishal noticed. He sat up, picked up the candle and looked at her shoes. “Wait, you did a double knot? That's tricky. You made both loops.” Preeti's smile came back. “I practised all day.”

qa.q: What had Preeti done herself?
qa.a: Tied her shoelaces.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when her smile faded?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and let down, because the flat “Hmm, good” without a look felt like he didn't care.

qa.q: What did Vishal do that helped, even though he was exhausted?
qa.a: He noticed her face, looked properly at her shoes, and praised exactly what she did.

qa.q: What would change if Vishal hadn't noticed?
qa.a: Preeti might have gone to bed feeling her effort didn't matter, and stopped showing him things.

grounding: After a long day, a father's flat praise falls flat for his preschooler, and specific words about what she did land better.

passage: In the city school's KG room, Gopika finished a hard jigsaw puzzle. Wasim Sir walked past. “Good job,” he said without stopping. Gopika looked after him. The next day she finished another. This time Wasim Sir knelt beside her, smiled, and said, “You kept trying even when the sky pieces all looked the same. You sorted them by colour first.” Gopika sat up straight. “I did the edges first too.” “Clever plan.” She started another puzzle straight away.

qa.q: What did Gopika sort by colour?
qa.a: The sky pieces.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she looked after Wasim Sir the first day?
qa.a: She probably felt a little disappointed or unsure, since his quick “Good job” didn't show he had really noticed.

qa.q: What made the second praise land better?
qa.a: Wasim Sir knelt, smiled and named exactly what she did, her effort and her colour plan.

qa.q: How might Wasim Sir see Gopika starting another puzzle straight away?
qa.a: He likely feels pleased, seeing that specific praise encouraged her to keep going.

grounding: A preschooler reads praise by tone and attention, and specific words about her effort land better than a passing “Good job.”

passage:
"Mama, look at my tower!"

Reena didn't look up from her phone. "Good job."

Tushar's smile faded. "You didn't even look."

"I did, beta..."

"You didn't. Your face didn't move."

Reena put the phone down and came over. She crouched and really looked. "Oh, I see. You put the big blocks at the bottom so it doesn't wobble. And you made a flag from paper on the top."

Tushar's smile came back. "The flag was the hardest part!"

"I can tell. You tried three times, didn't you?"

"Four!"

qa.q: What did Tushar make from paper for the top of the tower?
qa.a: A flag.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when Reena said "Good job" without looking?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and hurt, because he read her flat face and voice as not really caring. His smile faded before he said so.

qa.q: Why did Reena's second praise land better?
qa.a: It was specific about what he had done, big blocks at the bottom and the paper flag, and she was really looking, so it felt real and noticed his effort.

qa.q: How does Reena see the moment when Tushar says "Your face didn't move"?
qa.a: She is probably a bit caught out and sorry, which is why she puts the phone down and gives him her full attention.

grounding: It shows a young child reading flat praise as empty from tone and face, and specific words about what he did landing better.
